description.narrative: Our Voices Our Futures (OVOF) will use capacity-building and convenings among feminist movements to strengthen and build movements within countries and across regions, while also link feminist movements to relevant actors, such as internet rights’ movements, Dutch allies and progressive policymakers. OVOF believes in strengthening movements from within, to create more inclusive, powerful and resilient movements. To influence laws and policies at national and international levels, OVOF sees this as the only sustainable mitigation strategy in relation to the increasing power of anti-rights and anti-gender forces

UHAI partner organized monthly safe spaces for Female Sex Workers Who Use and Inject Drugs (FSWUID) to discuss their lived realities and strengthen their capacity to speak out and advocate for their rights. These spaces served as platforms for empowerment and peer-led dialogue on key issues such as access to SRHR services—including contraception, emergency care, and safe abortion—mental health and psychosocial support, legal rights and social protection, gender-based violence prevention, and the impact of punitive laws. Through these sessions, FSWUID gained knowledge, built solidarity, and mobilized around grassroots advocacy campaigns calling for decriminalization of sex work and drug possession, protection of bodily autonomy, and mental health justice. The interventions significantly strengthened the resilience, legal empowerment, and collective voice of LBTQ+ persons and sex workers in Uganda. Through documentation, legal aid, and intergenerational dialogue, communities were equipped with tools to navigate the ongoing crisis, advocate for their rights, and mobilize around shared struggles. These efforts not only improved access to justice and mental health support but also deepened solidarity and movement-building at a time of heightened repression under the AHA 2023.UHAI partner documentated the lived experiences of Female Sex Workers Who Use and Inject Drugs (FSWWUID) capturing their challenges, needs, and rights violations. Of these, 14 stories were taken up by a law clinic, leading to the establishment of a weekly legal clinic. This legal clinic now operates every Friday, offering free legal advice and support to FSWUID—marking a key step toward improving access to justice for marginalized communities.UHAI partner conducted documentation, response and publication of human rights violations against sex workers and LBTQ+ women to support evidence-based advocacy. This included the development and deployment of a monitoring tool that captured 67 cases of violations included evictions, arrests, physical attacks, and public outings. The documentation culminated in the production of the first-ever violations report, which now serves as a critical resource for legal response, public awareness, and policy engagement to protect the rights of LBTQ+ women and sex worker communities in Uganda. In partnership with legal support organisations, the partner organized two legal aid clinics, providing legal assistance and raising awareness about the rights and legal protections available to sex workers. Across both sessions, the partner engaged directly with 29 sex workers to offer tailored support and build legal literacy within the community.

CFCS VIII Pan-African Activists panel discussion: Focused on highlighting key elements of the dynamic socio-political context in East African countries such as Uganda where polarised public discourse on the rights LGBTIQ+ persons fueled negative attitudes towards UHAI’s sexual and gender minority communities. On the panel was representation of UHAI’s structurally silenced women and communities. Resourcing for under-funded and under-resourced movements such as LBQGNC, was discussed as an area that needed much more proactive attention from funders and allied partners. The need for being considerate of the dynamics within East African SSW/C movements. The activists centred wellness in the resilience building of our communities that continue to be adversely affected by the various forms of violence they face in all spaces. Priorities for the Uganda SSC movements were highlighted as: Increased and sustained resourcing to support community-based healthcare services including HIV treatment and psychosocial support in anticipation of the gaps in service delivery to SSW/C in the wake of the passing and implementation of the AHA2023. There was an appeal to support strategising at national level that also links to regional and global advocacy spaces to support efforts by human rights defenders in Uganda pushing back against the AHA2023.Digital systems organisational audit: to enhance the holistic safety and security for staff, local partner was supported to conduct a digital security audit for staff in conjunction with Defenders Protection Initiative (DPI). Internal staff obtained up-to-date digital security and safegaurding knowledge in the face of increased online violence for instance censorship and surveillance currently targeting LBQ womxn and wider LGBTQ+ community during implementation of AHA2023.Compliance to legal requirements: local partner strategic litigation community based organisations to ascertain the position of the SSW-led organisation amidst the implementation of the AHA2023, which has introduced new regulations for organisations working on and supporting LGBTQ+ issues in Uganda

UHAI partner organized a virtual solidarity meeting with 58 participants and representatives from 20 organizations. The meeting focused on learning from senior LGBTIQ+ role models about surviving and resisting oppressive laws such as the Anti-Homosexuality Act (AHA) 2013 and the Anti-Pornography Act. Participants engaged in reflective discussions, shared lived experiences, and contributed recommendations for navigating the current AHA 2023 crisis. The session also mapped out existing community structures and strategies to strengthen preparedness for future crises. Additionally, a one-day virtual resilience-building training was conducted for 30 LBTQ+ and sex worker community leaders. The training covered tools and approaches for personal and organizational resilience, including strategies for self-care, collective healing, and resource mobilizationUHAI partner facilitated five wellness and safe space engagements—four virtual and one physical, reaching a total of 275 LBQ womxn. The wellness and safe space engagements sessions addressed critical issues such as mental health, menstrual health, legal and political updates on the Anti-Homosexuality Act, toxic family environments, and collective resilience. Through these spaces, LBQ womxn accessed psychosocial support, influenced programming priorities, and strengthened community solidarity amidst rising threats. Through its quarterly wellness meetups, The partner cultivated safe, affirming spaces where LBQ womxn could meaningfully connect, reflect, and recharge. These gatherings became vital spaces for nurturing belonging and building political consciousness, enabling participants to explore their identities, activism, and lived realities in community. The sessions went beyond emotional and psychosocial support, they evolved into hubs for leadership growth, knowledge exchange, and feminist storytelling. As a result, the initiative significantly strengthened mental well-being, fostered solidarity, and reinforced the power and necessity of community-led healing as a cornerstone of feminist organising.

Description for quantitative indicator: LBQTGNC pre-conference at CFCS VIII; FFP Conference (The Hague) Description for qualitative indicator: Due to the current hostile and dynamic operating environment in Uganda, national and local policy and legal spaces were not welcoming of members of sexual and gender minorities and therefore SSW/C were not enabled to further their advocacy agenda to support their actions towards increasing the protection of their rights. LBQTGNC pre-conference at CFCS VIII: LBQGNC Africans constantly feel alienated in conferences due to lack of specific spaces for them to articulate their issues, network and strategize. The pre conference offered a space to create community, build radical sibling hood, experience joy, dance and share experiences as organizers within the African continent.Questions of creating Pan-African solidarity, language justice, reimagining alternative organizing, feminist leadership, power and funding and love and empathy for each other dominated the two-day pre-conference. Language has been a barrier in creating solidarity, and leaves the movement more porous and vulnerable. In terms of Pan-African solidarity, there is also a realization that mainstream feminist movements are sometimes hesitant to show up for LBQGNC people even though they (LBQGNC people) show up for them on issues such as GBV and Femicide.LBQGNC groups and organizations in the continent are underfunded. There is a tension between transformational work steeped in feminist praxis and the work of survival. Most funding structures are mainly heteropatriarchal and capitalistic structures while we try to break those structures. Money is a source of power, and the lack of it has further marginalized the LBQGNC movement, hindering the work and stifling their voice. The little funding has put organizers in a state of competition as opposed to compassion with each other, leading to a lot of hurt and harm. Healing and repair needs to be done to foster actual movement building and create a stronger LBQGNC movement in Africa. Feminist partners involved: AMwA (Akina Mama wa Africa) and Planned Parenthood office in Kenya.FFP Conference (The Hague): UHAI participated in advocacy initiatives with activists from SSC engaging in advocacy initiatives at national level that address the strategic advocacy and communication supporting the pushback against the AHA2023 and building the resilience of UHAI’s movements in Uganda. We were part of the advocacy video titled “Our Voices Our Futures - Feminist Foreign Policy” - UHAI’s contribution highlighted the need for feminist thinking in global policy processes because the norms on human rights are set at global level and affect the way policies are developed at national and local levels in Uganda.

Against the background of passing and implementation of the Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023, the partner embarked on a journey to capture the untold stories and vibrant experiences within the intersection of queerness and sports through the "Can We Play?" documentary. This documentary sheds light on the lived realities of queer individuals in sports; it was not just a deliberate endeavor to innovatively fuel our profound act of activism in the face of draconian laws but also amplify these stories. The documentary will further support the partner's advocacy initiatives, challenge systemic biases, and foster inclusivity within the sports landscape.Its major aims are to illuminate triumphs and challenges, celebrate diversity, break down barriers, highlight the resilience of LBTQI people in sports, and amplify the voices that redefine what it means to be an athlete in a more inclusive and accepting sporting landscape.
